title: Embedding rate-fence and burst reservation for stable throughput
creator: Asha Patel
description: Problem: We observe recurring P99+ latency spikes and throughput collapses on the embeddings endpoint during bursty traffic from multi-tenant customers. Root causes identified: coarse global rate limits, tokenization variance leading to uneven batching, and the autoscaler reacting too slowly to short bursts. Impact: production customers experience 2–5x latency increases during bursts and occasional 429 amplifications that cascade into reduced overall throughput.
goal: Introduce a rate-fence and burst reservation layer combined with token-aware admission control so that embedding endpoints can absorb short bursts without violating tenant SLAs or causing global throughput regressions. Provide a capacity-planning model and synthetic load generator to validate behavior across tenant mixes.
acceptance_criteria: P99 embedding latency for 99% of traffic remains <= 150ms under 3x baseline burst for 30s windows
No increase in global error rate (5xx) during burst absorption compared to baseline
Autoscaler reacts within configured headroom and does not trigger mass scale-down during burst windows
Documentation and runbook published; post-deploy dashboard shows reserve utilization and per-tenant token-buckets
proposed_solution_outline: 1) Rate-fence: per-tenant token-buckets with refill tied to SLA tier + short-term burst reservations
2) Burst reservation pool: small global reserve that can be loaned to high-priority tenants for 10–60s windows
3) Token-aware admission and batching: estimate token count at admission, form batches with token budget heuristics, reject early with clear retry-after when over budget
4) Autoscaler tuning: introduce short-window predictive component using the synthetic load generator signals to provision headroom proactively
5) Capacity model: Monte Carlo simulation for tenant mixes, integrated into capacity planning docs
6) Metrics & dashboards: reserve utilization, per-tenant token-bucket fill, admission rejects, batching efficiency, cost-per-1k-embeddings
tradeoffs_and_risks: Tight rate-fences improve stability but can increase rejected requests for noisy tenants — mitigated with tiered burst allowances
Global burst pool reduces rejections but increases cost if frequently used; will gate by SLAs and budget thresholds
Token estimation at admission adds extra CPU work in the router; need benchmarks to ensure it doesn't become a new bottleneck
Predictive autoscaling can over-provision if signals are noisy — we'll combine with conservative decay and override thresholds

metrics_to_track: burst-reserve utilization (percentage of time and capacity consumed)
batching efficiency (tokens per batch, wasted slots)
implementation_notes: Use existing router admission hooks; add token-estimator that mirrors tokenizer rounding used by model runtime
Persist token-bucket state in in-memory shard with periodic checkpointing to Redis for cross-node failover
Expose a /reserve API for internal components to request short-term burst capacity with TTL
Start with conservative default refill rates derived from typical tenant profiles (seeded from last 90 days of usage)
Feature-flag the burst pool and predictive autoscaler; canary to 5% tenants before wider rollout
testing_plan: Unit tests for token estimation and bucket accounting
Integration tests: simulate multi-tenant bursts with synthetic load generator; assert latency and reject bounds
Chaos test: drop reserved pool node and ensure graceful degradation
Canary: ramp from 1% to 5% to 25% tenants over 72 hours with dashboards monitored
